Tools: Microsoft Visio/Word, Project and Excel. **AI use:** not permitted for any part of the report. ::: []{#sec-precitech-case} ::: {.callout-note} ## Case study — Précitech Components: new shaft-kit assembly & packing cell **Précitech Components** is a Tier-1 automotive supplier in Granby, Québec. Its CNC turning cells produce transmission **shaft blanks** (AISI 4140 steel, Ø 25.000 mm ± 0.050 mm) for a major OEM customer. The OEM now wants the shafts delivered as a **ready-to-install kit** rather than as loose blanks, so Précitech is adding a **manual kitting, sub-assembly and packing cell** immediately downstream of the CNC turning cells. **One shaft kit contains:** 1 machined shaft blank, 2 tapered roller bearings, 1 retaining ring, 1 lip seal, 1 dowel pin, 1 desiccant sachet — placed in a moulded tray inside a labelled carton. The exact part numbers, quantities and shaft dimensions are on the assembly drawing ([410-2365, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-410-2365-shaft-kit-assembly-RevB.pdf)) and shaft detail drawing ([205-5478, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-205-5478-shaft-RevB.pdf)) — you need both for this lab. **Target output:** 250 kits/day on one 8-hour shift. **Process outline:** finished blanks arrive from the CNC cells on a trolley; bought-in components (bearings, rings, seals, pins) are held in a small storage rack that is replenished from the main warehouse when stock falls to a reorder level; an operator picks the components for one kit, presses the two bearings onto the shaft, fits the retaining ring and lip seal, inspects the assembly against a checklist, places it in a tray, closes and labels the carton, and stages it for the shipping dock. Plant manager **Sophie Tran** has asked you to produce the engineering documentation package for this cell **before it is built**. *This is the same plant used in the machine-learning labs (see [Machine Learning](#sec-chap-ml-lab)), which build a predictive-maintenance proof of concept for Précitech's CNC turning cells.* ::: #### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-outcomes} After this lab you should be able to: - Explain terms such as HSE, Basic Engineering Design Data (BEDD), Front-End Engineering Design (FEED), fast-tracking, project schedule and General Arrangement (GA) drawing. - Produce a specification sheet and a bill of materials for a manufactured product. - Build a task list / process-flow chart with durations and turn it into a project schedule and Gantt chart in Microsoft Project. - Draft a production-facility layout drawing showing product in/out, stations, storage, and material and people flow, and mark starvation / blockage risk points. - Compare a highly automated (turntable) cell against a manual U-cell and justify a configuration choice for a given volume, timeline and labour situation. - Complete an HSE risk assessment for a manual assembly cell. ::: #### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-prep} - Read the **case study** above and Unit 2 content on the basics of process engineering and design. - Review the assembly drawing ([410-2365, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-410-2365-shaft-kit-assembly-RevB.pdf)) and the shaft detail drawing ([205-5478, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-205-5478-shaft-RevB.pdf)) — you need the part numbers, quantities, materials and key dimensions from these for your spec sheet and BOM. Two realistic options are on the table for a 250-kit/day, single-shift cell: **Option A — highly automated: rotary turntable, 6–7 stations.** An indexing turntable carries the shaft through fixed stations (press bearing 1, press bearing 2, fit retaining ring, fit seal, insert dowel pin + desiccant, inspect, place in tray / close carton), with **one operator** at a single load/unload station. each week every group is at a different one of the three labs, and each group starts at a different lab, so by the end of week three every student has completed all three (see [Materials-testing rotation](#sec-materials-rotation)). Your instructor posts your group and your starting lab on FOL. ::: {.callout-important} ## Safety in the materials laboratory Wear **safety glasses and safety footwear** — you will not be admitted without them. Do not handle dry ice with bare hands: use insulated gloves and tongs. Keep alcohol off your skin (it is absorbed through it), keep etchant off your skin, and stay clear of the pendulum's swing path in the Charpy lab. ::: Testing is done in teams so that everyone can see the test, but **each student writes and submits their own report** on the template provided on FOL. ### Hardness Testing: Rockwell and Brinell {#sec-lab-hardness} ::: {.lab-overview} Hardness is a material's resistance to indentation, and it is the quickest test of what a heat treatment has done to a steel. You measure the hardness of three steel specimens — **annealed**, **quenched (hardened)** and **normalized** — with two methods: the **Rockwell** tester (choosing the right scale, minor load and major load) and the **Brinell** tester (measuring the indentation diameter and converting it to a Brinell number). You average repeated readings, convert between scales, calculate the percentage deviation and the reproducibility of each method, and explain why the three heat treatments give different hardness. **AI use:** not permitted for the readings and calculations. Your written answers must be your own. ::: #### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-outcomes} After this lab you should be able to: - Carry out Rockwell and Brinell hardness tests correctly, including scale and load selection. - Convert between Rockwell and Brinell values using a conversion chart. - Compare the reproducibility of the two methods for each specimen. - Explain annealing, quenching and normalizing and relate each to the hardness you measured. ::: #### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-prep} - Read your notes on the heat treatment of steel — annealing, quenching and normalizing — and the difference between the Rockwell B and C scales. - Review the definition of range (maximum minus minimum), which you use as your measure of reproducibility. - Download the report template from FOL (*Hardness Testing*). ::: #### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-materials} - Rockwell hardness tester (with ball and diamond indenters) and Brinell hardness tester with a measuring microscope - Annealed, quenched and normalized steel specimens - Rockwell–Brinell conversion chart (or an online source) - Safety glasses and safety footwear - The hardness report template from FOL ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"} Test each specimen with both methods, record the readings in Tables 1 and 2 of the template, complete the calculations, answer the questions and write the conclusions on how closely the two methods agree and how reproducible each is. Submit your own report in the FOL quiz. The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file. ::: ### Tensile and Microhardness Testing of Case-Hardened Steel {#sec-lab-tensile} ::: {.lab-overview} A case-hardened part is hard on the outside and tough in the core. You examine the microstructure of the **case** and the **core** of a case-hardened steel (AISI 1566) and run a **Vickers microhardness traverse** from the surface inwards in 0.5 mm steps, converting each indentation diameter to a Vickers and then a Rockwell number. You plot hardness against depth and read off the **effective case depth** (where hardness falls to HRC 50) and the **true case depth** (HRC 40). You then test tensile specimens, plot their stress–strain curves and use them to decide which material is the most brittle, the most ductile and the toughest, and you calculate stress and strain for each. **AI use:** not permitted for the readings, calculations and graphs. Your written conclusions must be your own. ::: #### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-outcomes} After this lab you should be able to: - Explain what case hardening does and how the microstructure of case and core differ. - Perform a Vickers microhardness traverse, convert the results to Rockwell numbers and plot a hardness profile. - Determine the effective and true case depths from the profile. - Explain what a tensile test measures — yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility — and calculate stress and strain from load and extension. - Compare materials from their stress–strain curves: brittle versus ductile, and toughness as the area under the curve. ::: #### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-prep} - Read the **Tensile Testing and Microhardness Testing of Case-Hardened Material** slides from FOL — loading, stress, strain, the stress–strain curve, what the tensile test reveals, and how Vickers microhardness works. - Review the formulas for engineering stress (load ÷ original area) and strain (extension ÷ original gauge length). - Download the report template from FOL (*Tensile and MicroHardness Test*). ::: #### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-materials} - Case-hardened AISI 1566 specimen (mounted and polished) and a metallurgical microscope - Vickers microhardness tester - Tensile testing machine with data acquisition, and the tensile specimens - Vickers-to-Rockwell conversion chart - Safety glasses and safety footwear - The tensile and microhardness report template from FOL ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"} Record the metallography sketches, complete the hardness table (depth, indentation diameter, Vickers, Rockwell), plot the two hardness graphs, state the effective and true case depths, then complete the tensile results and conclusions in the template. Submit your own report in the FOL quiz. The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file. ::: ### Charpy Impact Testing and the Ductile-to-Brittle Transition {#sec-lab-charpy} ::: {.lab-overview} Some steels are tough at room temperature and shatter when cold — the failure mode behind brittle-fracture disasters in cold-weather structures. You break notched **Charpy** bars of **AISI 1018 hot-rolled** and **cold-rolled** steel in a pendulum impact tester at temperatures from well below freezing to above boiling-water heat, recording the energy absorbed at each. Low temperatures come from a bath of alcohol and **dry ice**; high temperatures from heated water. You plot impact toughness against temperature for each steel, read off the **ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT)**, and compare the fracture surfaces (fine granular for brittle fracture, necking for ductile). **AI use:** not permitted for the readings, calculations and graphs. Your written conclusions must be your own. ::: #### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-outcomes} After this lab you should be able to: - Explain what the Charpy value measures and how rate of loading, temperature and a notch affect toughness. - Conduct Charpy tests safely at controlled temperatures, transferring the specimen and striking it within the time limit. - Plot impact toughness against temperature and determine the DBTT for each steel. - Describe and explain brittle and ductile fracture surfaces. - Explain which crystal structure is susceptible to low-temperature brittleness and why the two steels differ. ::: #### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-prep} - Read the **Material Toughness, Charpy Impact Test, and the Ductile to Brittle Temperature Transition** slides from FOL — toughness, strain rate, notch effect, the Charpy test and the DBTT. - Read the safety rules for the pendulum tester and for dry ice before the lab. - Download the report template from FOL (*Charpy Impact Test*). ::: #### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted} ::: {.lab-materials} - Charpy pendulum impact tester - Notched AISI 1018 hot-rolled and cold-rolled Charpy specimens - Temperature baths: alcohol and **dry ice** for the low temperatures (about −60, −40, −20 and 0 °C), room temperature, and heated water for the high temperatures (about 60 and 100 °C); a thermometer and tongs - Insulated gloves, safety glasses and safety footwear - The Charpy report template from FOL ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"} Hold each specimen at its test temperature for several minutes so the whole bar is at temperature, and break it **within five seconds** of removing it from the bath. The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file. ::: --- ## Virtual Welding {#sec-labs-welding} Six progressive labs in **GMAW** (gas metal arc welding, often called MIG) on the **Lincoln Electric VRTEX 360+** virtual-reality welding simulator. There is no arc, no fume and no wasted metal: you practise on a simulated coupon while the machine tracks your gun position, angle and travel speed and **scores every weld**. The process is the one automated and robotic welding cells replicate, so these labs give you the operator's view of what a welding cell has to get right. In every lab you set the machine up **from a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS)** — the document that fixes the shielding gas and flow rate, wire feed speed, voltage and polarity for the joint — weld the coupon, and save your best scored result. The labs share one routine (start-up, login, set-up screens, monitor screens), so the first lab teaches it in detail and the later labs reuse it.
